title: I Installed a DIY Mini-Split—Here's What It Cost to Run
summary: An Arizona DIYer reviews three years of a self-installed dual-zone mini-split, comparing DIY and professional install costs and claiming a four-year payback.

assertions.quote: $500 a year it take 4 years to pay back the unit.

verdicts.note: Self-installing avoids labour markup, but refrigerant handling and warranty terms often require a licensed technician.

assertions.quote: extreme hot and cold outside temperatures will affect the mini split's efficiency.
Equipment that is oversized won't run efficiently, and will likely cause a short cycling, poor humidity control, and a waste of energy.
your home should have a secondary heating and cooling source, like electric baseboard heaters, a furnace, or even a portable air conditioner

verdicts.note: Cold-climate units cope alone in many places, but backup heat is common practice where design temperatures fall below the unit's rated range.
The ductless unit's capacity fell to about 20% of rated below -20F, and the authors conclude these units should not be used without backup at extreme temperatures (below -15F).

Mini-splits supplied only about 14% of installed heating capacity and nearly always ran alongside another system as secondary or spot heating; this reflects how they were sized and used, not proof that one could not carry the load.

assertions.quote: this is the only thing that we use to heat and cool our home.
